meta.description: ‘No man is free who is not master of himself’ is a doubtful, Stobaeus-preserved fragment in Oldfather’s 1928 Loeb Epictetus — not securely his.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'No man is free who is not master of himself'?
meta.ogDescription: It reads as pure Epictetus, but the line is Fragment 35 among his ‘doubtful and spurious’ fragments — Oldfather’s 1928 translation, via Stobaeus.

answer.label: Not securely Epictetus — a doubtful fragment
answer.authorDates: c. 50 – c. 135 AD · Greek Stoic philosopher, born enslaved
answer.sourceLine: This exact English line is W. A. Oldfather’s 1928 Loeb translation of a Greek maxim — Οὐδεὶς ἐλεύθερος ἑαυτοῦ μὴ κρατῶν — that survives only as Fragment 35 in the ‘doubtful and spurious’ section of Epictetus’s fragments. These are sayings gathered centuries later by the anthologist Stobaeus, not passages from the Discourses or Handbook that Arrian actually recorded. Its authenticity as Epictetus’s own words is not established; in Stobaeus the same maxim is elsewhere attached to Pythagoras, and Oldfather judged its style alien to Epictetus. The confident “Epictetus said this” you see everywhere overstates a fragment his own modern editor flagged as doubtful.

source.excerpt: Οὐδεὶς ἐλεύθερος ἑαυτοῦ μὴ κρατῶν. — “No man is free who is not master of himself.”
trail: The line is catalogued as Fragment 35 in the ‘Doubtful fragments’ of Epictetus on Wikiquote, with the Greek Οὐδεὶς ἐλεύθερος ἑαυτοῦ μὴ κρατῶν.
In W. A. Oldfather’s 1928 Loeb translation it sits under ‘Doubtful and Spurious Fragments’ on Wikisource, worded exactly as popularly quoted.
The same wording (in George Long’s translation) of the fragment appears in the Perseus Digital Library’s text of the Fragments.
These maxims were gathered centuries after Epictetus by the anthologist Stobaeus — a provenance and authenticity discussed at Neologikon.

author.name: Epictetus
author.heading: About Epictetus
author.metaLine: c. 50 – c. 135 AD · Greek Stoic philosopher, born enslaved
author.bio: Epictetus was a Stoic philosopher born into slavery at Hierapolis (in modern Turkey) around 50 AD; freed as an adult, he taught in Rome and later at Nicopolis in Greece. He wrote nothing himself — his teaching survives because his pupil Arrian transcribed it as the Discourses and the Enchiridion (Handbook). A cluster of shorter maxims, of very uneven authenticity, was later gathered under his name by the anthologist Stobaeus; the line quoted here belongs to that doubtful outer layer, not to the works Arrian recorded.

misattribution.heading: Attribution check
misattribution.intro: The line circulates as settled Epictetus. It is really a maxim from the doubtful margins of his fragment corpus, in a specific modern translator’s words.

items.why: It is not in the works Arrian recorded. It appears only as Fragment 35 among the ‘doubtful and spurious fragments’ — maxims collected by the 5th-century anthologist Stobaeus.
The exact English one-liner is Oldfather’s Loeb rendering of Οὐδεὶς ἐλεύθερος ἑαυτοῦ μὴ κρατῶν; Wikiquote lists it as his translation. Epictetus taught in Greek, not English.
Sites present it as firmly Epictetus, but his own modern editor grouped it with fragments of doubtful authenticity, and in Stobaeus the same maxim is elsewhere credited to Pythagoras.

misattribution.truthLine: It is a genuinely Epictetan idea — freedom as self-mastery runs through the Discourses — but this exact sentence survives only as a doubtful, possibly spurious fragment in Oldfather’s 1928 translation, not a securely attested quotation.

context.heading: Why the idea still reads as Epictetus
lead: The thought lands because it is Stoic to the core. For Epictetus, freedom is not political or physical but internal: a person is free only insofar as they master their own judgments, desires and aversions — the things “up to us” — rather than being ruled by them. Whole stretches of the Discourses argue exactly this, that the enslaved can be free and the powerful can be slaves to their own passions.

So the one-liner distills real Epictetan doctrine. What it cannot claim is a secure textual pedigree: it comes not from Arrian’s record of Epictetus’s lectures but from the later, unreliable anthology tradition, where sayings drifted between authors and where this maxim is grouped with the doubtful and spurious.
detailsBody: Epictetus’s fragments were preserved mainly in the Anthology of Stobaeus, a late-antique compiler. Modern editors (Schenkl, Oldfather) separated a small set of plausibly genuine fragments from a larger body of doubtful and spurious ones; this line falls in the latter group.

Fragment numbering varies by edition — it is no. 35 in Oldfather’s book but appears under a different number in the Perseus text — which is one reason the same saying can look more ‘canonical’ than its authenticity warrants.
context.pull: Freedom as self-mastery is pure Epictetus — this exact sentence is not securely his.
